claims.text: A CALPHAD–machine-learning hybrid workflow will accurately predict melting temperature, entropy of fusion, and heat capacity for refractory high-entropy alloys.
High-throughput CALPHAD calculations can generate training values of Tm, ΔSfus, and Cp over a representative multicomponent composition set.
A machine-learning surrogate can efficiently screen the vast HEA composition space while CALPHAD is reserved for selected candidates.
Mean elemental melting point, configurational entropy, mixing enthalpy, and atomic-size mismatch are sufficient descriptors for predicting the proposed melting properties.
Rule-of-mixtures approaches fail to capture nonlinear melting-temperature depression and complex entropy contributions in multicomponent alloys.
The inadequacy of rule-of-mixtures approaches becomes more pronounced as the number of principal elements increases.
The configurational entropy of an equimolar N-component alloy is R ln N.
Competition between configurational entropy and mixing enthalpy controls stabilization of a disordered solid solution against ordered intermetallic phases.
The number of distinct binary interaction pairs in an N-component alloy increases as N(N-1)/2.
Increasing the number of elements rapidly increases the probability of forming intermetallic compounds having strongly negative formation enthalpies.
Formation of these intermetallic compounds depresses the solidus temperature.
Vibrational entropy is smaller than configurational entropy in concentrated solid-solution alloys.
CALPHAD captures nonlinear interaction thermodynamics, while the machine-learning model can extrapolate those trends to unexplored compositions.
In refractory systems, increasing N from 3 to 6 will reduce Tm from approximately 2925 °C to approximately 2400 °C.
Entropy of fusion will be dominated by R ln N configurational entropy, with only a small vibrational correction.
Heat capacity can be represented as an elemental weighted average with an anharmonicity correction.
The workflow will identify alloys with Tm above 2000 °C and high solid-solution stability.
For high-N systems, the hybrid workflow will outperform rule-of-mixtures Tm predictions by more than 15% in accuracy.
The method is valid for single-phase BCC, FCC, or HCP solid solutions.
The method fails for systems dominated by complex intermetallic or amorphous structures with ill-defined liquidus–solidus gaps or anomalous fusion entropy.
